child_drafts.title: Education Department Workforce Falls Roughly 45% From 2024 Level

This child documents the staffing change; it does not combine that outcome with every separate transfer agreement, hearing statement, or budget proposal.
child_drafts.description_long: At a May 14, 2026 House education committee hearing, Education Secretary Linda McMahon defended the administration’s effort to wind down the Department of Education. KPBS, reporting on NPR material and citing Office of Personnel Management data, said department staffing had declined from roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 to about 2,300 in 2026, or approximately 45%. The report also said more than 100 programs and department obligations had been shifted to other agencies, including elementary and secondary education functions to the Department of Labor and family-engagement work to Health and Human Services. Those figures describe a cumulative workforce and program-transfer change as of the report date, not one July 2026 action. The article separately covers McMahon’s congressional testimony, the proposed FY2027 budget and possible future transfers. They should remain distinct unless separately sourced and dated. The staffing count is attributed to OPM data cited by the reporters; it should not be presented as an independent audit or as proof of motive.

child_drafts.title: Court Sets Aside HUD's 2025 Continuum of Care Funding Notices
child_drafts.description_short: A federal court ruled that HUD's November and December 2025 Continuum of Care notices violated the Administrative Procedure Act and set them aside.
child_drafts.description_medium: On June 29, 2026, a federal court set aside HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices. California’s attorney general said the ruling found the notices unlawful under the Administrative Procedure Act and preserved billions in homelessness funding. This decision concerned FY2025 notices; the separate August 2026 ruling addressed a later FY2026 notice.
child_drafts.description_long: A federal court ruled on June 29, 2026 that HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices could not stand. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found that HUD had made material changes to the program without following the Administrative Procedure Act. The ruling set aside the notices and preserved approximately $3.6 billion in funding for homelessness programs while litigation proceeded. The Continuum of Care program funds local and regional systems that coordinate housing and services for people experiencing homelessness. The June decision concerned the prior fiscal year’s competition and its funding notices. It should be described as a court ruling about those particular notices, rather than a blanket reversal of all HUD policy changes or a finding on every asserted consequence for people in permanent supportive housing. A later, separate August 2026 decision addressed HUD’s FY2026 notice and should retain its own date and procedural posture.

child_drafts.title: Court Sets Aside HUD's FY2026 Continuum of Care Notice
child_drafts.description_medium: On August 7, 2026, a federal court blocked HUD’s FY2026 Continuum of Care notice changes. California’s attorney general reported that the court found the policy revisions unlawful and preserved permanent supportive housing funding. HUD’s program page confirms the program’s annual competition context; the court ruling remains a separate action from the June decision about FY2025 notices.
child_drafts.description_long: On August 7, 2026, a federal court blocked changes HUD had made to the FY2026 Continuum of Care funding competition. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found the administration’s revisions unlawful and prevented the new notice from diverting funds away from permanent supportive housing. HUD describes Continuum of Care as a competitive program that supports community systems serving people experiencing homelessness. The August ruling concerned the FY2026 notice and followed a June ruling that set aside HUD’s earlier FY2025 notices. These are separate court orders involving different annual funding competitions; they should not be collapsed into one ruling or described as three separate wins without identifying the orders. The state release characterizes the result as protecting permanent supportive housing, while the HUD competition page supplies the administrative program context. The available sources do not establish the held claim that exactly 97,000 people would be pushed onto the street.

child_drafts.description_long: In a March 2026 analysis, the Brennan Center for Justice examined the Trump administration’s requests for emergency relief from the Supreme Court, often called the emergency or shadow docket. The Center reported that the administration had sought emergency intervention more than 30 times during its first 14 months and later specified a tally of 34 applications. Its analysis compared the frequency and outcomes with prior administrations and said Trump’s administration had succeeded in a large share of its requests. Those numbers are the Center’s own research and depend on how it classifies applications and grants; they are not an official Supreme Court statistic. The analysis concerns repeated litigation requests across multiple cases, rather than one specific lawsuit or the separate DOJ misconduct complaint against Judge Boasberg. A factual event entry should name the Brennan Center as the source of the tally, state its measurement period, and avoid treating its “abuse” characterization as a neutral court finding.

child_drafts.description_long: Howard Lutnick’s ethics and financial disclosure records show a series of divestitures after he entered government service. ProPublica’s disclosure page lists assets and transactions, while a later SEC filing records reported transactions in securities connected to his prior business interests. A corrected entry should identify the disclosure and filing as records of divestiture transactions, attribute any estimated value to the relevant source, and avoid presenting temporal coincidence as evidence of insider knowledge.

child_drafts.title: Trump DOJ orders review of FBI personnel tied to January 6 cases before Patel takes office
child_drafts.description_short: Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove ordered personnel actions and a review of FBI employees who worked on January 6 cases.
child_drafts.description_medium: On January 31, 2025, Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed personnel actions and asked the FBI to identify employees who had worked on January 6 cases. Reuters reported the order and related dismissals before Kash Patel became FBI director. It is distinct from later personnel removals under Patel and does not establish that Trump personally directed those actions.
child_drafts.description_long: On January 31, 2025, Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed the FBI to take personnel actions and identify employees who had worked on investigations related to the January 6 attack on the Capitol. Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter, reported dismissals and ultimatums affecting FBI personnel and described a review of agents connected to the cases. The order preceded Kash Patel’s confirmation as FBI director in February, so it should not be characterized as an action Patel carried out after taking office. The reporting also does not establish that Trump personally issued the order or that every employee associated with January 6 was dismissed. This is one discrete early personnel review; later dismissals of senior FBI officials and agents occurred in separate periods and should be recorded independently. The description should attribute details based on unnamed sources to Reuters and avoid converting the reported review into proof of a bureau-wide removal of hundreds of agents.

child_drafts.description_long: The FBI dismissed three senior officials in August 2025, including Brian Driscoll, who had served as acting director, according to The Washington Post. The report said the officials had at times clashed with the Trump administration and described the departures as part of a broader reshaping of the bureau under Director Kash Patel. It was a separate personnel action from Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove’s January 31 request to identify FBI employees involved in January 6 cases. The report does not establish the sweeping claim that hundreds of agents had already been fired for insufficient loyalty, nor does it show that all three dismissals were based on the same investigation or rationale. Later reporting about agents tied to the Mar-a-Lago investigation covers another date and another group. A corrected entry should identify the three senior officials, use the August date, and attribute the reported context rather than state motive as settled fact.

child_drafts.description_long: In February 2026, the FBI dismissed at least a dozen agents whose work had been connected directly or indirectly to the investigation of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, The Washington Post reported. The article describes the dismissals under FBI Director Kash Patel and traces some agents’ roles to the investigation of Trump’s handling of classified records. This is a later action than the January 2025 review of personnel who worked on January 6 cases and the August 2025 removal of three senior officials. The source supports the reported count and connection to the Mar-a-Lago investigation, but it does not establish every broader assertion in the original entry about hundreds of agents, a counterterrorism staffing crisis, or an identical loyalty criterion for all personnel decisions. A separate child should keep this February 2026 group and date distinct and attribute the count to the Post’s reporting. Any additional claims about litigation, reasons, or consequences require their own sources.
